chapter: Decca records, the Savoy and Moe Gale
title: The Cassadel in Tulsa expecting a white band
summary: In Tulsa band members first heard Confessin' the Blues on a jukebox, and the club owner had expected a white band because of the McShann name.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: And while we got out -- book was why we discontinued they had the book going and they had these head tunes going all the time too so we played a place in Tulsa, Oklahoma, that's the first time we heard Confessing Blues on the record. And somebody went downtown in Tulsa and they says, man, -- a couple of guys in the band, they went down there and they heard somebody in a booth playing it and they went over and listened and they said, that's us. So they bought the record and brought the record back out.

So that was the first time we had ever heard it, you know, we were placing in Tulsa at a place called the Cassadel. The funniest thing about the place where we was playing, they thought they was getting a white band when we came in there and -- because of the name McShann and the night we opened we took the instruments and stuff out, so they figured well, these guys are bringing the instruments in. So we stood around there, he says when the band coming. I said the band's already here. He said, the band's already here, what do you mean?

I says well, the guys are coming on in. He says, I know they set the band up, but I don't see none of the musicians. I say here we are. He say, wait a minute. He says, I'm looking for Jay McShann, and I said well, I'm Jay.
He says, oh, no, don't tell me, wait a minute. I said, yeah, what were you expecting, and he says, we were expecting
a white band. I said oh.
Was it a social dance or something.

This was a club that had been there for a long time, but see, they had never had a colored band in there, but he thought he was buying a white band because of the name you know. We got so and so for you. Okay. And so the lady, the secretary she said, 'well, listen, what are you going to do. You can't call nobody else now. These guys are already set up, let them go on and play.' So he says, 'I don't know what to do. I don't know what my customers are going to say.' She said, 'don't worry about that, they're going to want some music. Let them go on and play.'
So we went on and played, so after we played that night, the people liked the band, so he says, okay, we'll go for the finish.
That was real funny experience, but anyway that's the time the Confessin' Blues really sold, and Walter Brown --
